evidence.claim: The Oregon Trail Historic Byway follows U.S. 26 west from the Nebraska border to Dwyer Junction, connecting Torrington, Lingle, Fort Laramie and Guernsey.
evidence.quote: The Oregon Trail Historic Byway begins on US 26 at the Wyoming/Nebraska border. From there it follows US 26 west through Torrington, Lingle, Fort Laramie, and Guernsey to the intersection with Interstate 25 at Dwyer Junction.

evidence.claim: Between Torrington and Guernsey, the drive follows the North Platte River corridor.
evidence.quote: motorists will be following the path of the historic Oregon and Mormon Trail as they make their way along the banks of the North Platte River

evidence.claim: Wyoming’s tourism office gives this historic byway a length of 57 miles and advises an hour and a half without stops.
evidence.quote: The total length is 57 miles and should take an hour and a half without stopping.

evidence.claim: Register Cliff rises a hundred feet above the valley floor, with emigrants’ inscriptions still visible.
evidence.quote: A sandstone precipice rising one hundred feet from the valley floor of the North Platte River, it is one of three main sites along the Oregon Trail where emigrants left inscriptions, still visible today.

evidence.claim: The older trail carried traders, trappers and missionaries before the wagon migrations of the 1840s.
evidence.quote: Traders, trappers, and missionaries used this route before 1841

evidence.claim: Near Guernsey, the route avoided marshy river ground by crossing a sandstone ridge.
evidence.quote: The trail ruts are 0.5 miles (0.80 km) long and are worn 2 to 6 feet (0.61 to 1.83 m) into a sandstone ridge. The route was chosen to avoid the marshy ground along the river.

evidence.claim: Wheels, animals and people wore down that rock during heavy use from 1841 to 1869.
evidence.quote: Here, wagon wheels, draft animals, and people wore down the trail into a sandstone ridge about two to six feet, during its heavy usage from 1841 to 1869.

evidence.claim: Completion of the Union Pacific Railroad in 1869 sharply reduced overland trail travel, though local use continued.
evidence.quote: With the completion of the Union Pacific Railroad in 1869, use of the trail as an overland route to the Pacific rapidly declined, although sections of it continued to be used locally for many years.

evidence.claim: Fort Laramie began as a private fur-trading post; the U.S. Army bought it in 1849.
evidence.quote: The fort was founded as a private trading post in the 1830s to service the overland fur trade; in 1849, it was purchased by the United States Army.

evidence.claim: The fort stood east of the long climb toward South Pass, an important Rocky Mountain crossing for wagon travelers.
evidence.quote: The site was located east of the long climb leading to the best and lowest crossing over the Rocky Mountains at South Pass and became a popular stop for migrants on the Oregon Trail.

evidence.claim: It became a stop for emigrant wagon trains and a military post during the Plains Indian Wars.
evidence.quote: Fort Laramie became a haven for gold seekers and weary emigrants, a station for the Pony Express and the Overland Stage, and served as an important military post during the Plains Indian Wars.

evidence.claim: Old Bedlam, built in 1849, housed officers who shared rooms and communal kitchens.

evidence.claim: Old Bedlam, built in 1849, housed officers who shared rooms and communal kitchens.
evidence.quote: Old Bedlam served as the original officer quarters for Fort Laramie. It was used by officers of various rank and marital status, since no other housing was yet available. Old Bedlam offered very little privacy utilizing public kitchen areas and soldiers often sharing rooms.

evidence.claim: The Army abandoned the fort in 1890.
evidence.quote: The fort was abandoned in 1890

evidence.claim: The surviving complex includes standing buildings and ruins, preserved by the National Park Service.
evidence.quote: The remaining structures are preserved as the Fort Laramie National Historic Site by the National Park Service.

evidence.claim: These are remnants of a larger post: the remaining structures represent only a third of the buildings once here.
evidence.quote: Many ruins of old structures are present at Fort Laramie Historic Site, with the remaining structures making up only a third of the buildings that were once at Fort Laramie.
